description: We’re a crew of 5 engineering students tackling the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. We're combining code, AI-assisted development, and interactive game mechanics to build an engaging space exploration experience for kids. Our squad is locked in and ready to build!
summary:
The Ares Protocol is a browser-based 3D learning game designed for children ages 7–12. Players travel from Earth to a fictional Mars outpost, where they explore, maintain essential systems and investigate the surface.

Instead of learning through text-heavy quizzes, players perform interactive tasks: clearing vents, replacing batteries, watering plants, preparing shelter and collecting specimens for microscope examination. Successful work restores resources and advances the mission. Meanwhile, life-support consumption and occasional hazards demonstrate why maintenance and preparation matter.

NASA models, imagery and space-weather resources connect the adventure to real exploration. Scientific observations are presented separately from simplified game mechanics.

Built with Vue, Three.js and Rapier, the project aims to make space engineering approachable through exploration, visible consequences and hands-on problem solving. It is an educational prototype, not professional astronaut training.
details:
The Ares Protocol turns the challenge of supporting human exploration into a hands-on 3D adventure for children ages 7–12.

Players begin with an interactive Earth launch, complete activities inside a spacecraft cabin and descend toward Mars. At the outpost, they can explore buildings, use an airlock, equip a spacesuit and approach physical machines to begin work.

The central learning experience is maintaining an interconnected base. Players clear air vents, replace and reconnect batteries, care for plants and reinforce shelter. Completing work restores resources or improves protection. Life-support consumption and occasional hazards create an opportunity cost: time spent investigating the surface is also time during which the base needs attention.

Exploration gives those systems a purpose. A driveable rover provides battery-powered transport to three practice survey locations. Players scan the surface, choose specimens within a two-slot cargo limit and return to the solar laboratory. There, they focus a microscope, capture an illustrated image, describe the grains and record an observation. Science rewards are awarded after examination, rather than simply for picking up an object.

Preparation also changes outcomes. Closing greenhouse shutters and securing equipment can prevent a dust fault. Power maintenance restores reserves and clears visible panel dust. These connections help players understand cause and effect through actions and feedback.

NASA resources provide scientific context and visual references. The science interface can request DONKI space-weather observations and NASA imagery, with archive or unavailable states when fresh responses cannot be obtained. Archived InSight weather information is identified separately. NASA observations do not determine the game’s hazard schedule, resource losses or simulated health conditions.

The application uses Vue 3 and TypeScript for its interface, Three.js for rendering and animation, and Rapier for movement and collisions. A Node.js API with PostgreSQL supports optional account-based progress saving. Guest play remains available.

Our creative approach combines exploration, physical-object interactions and short illustrated activities rather than relying on quizzes or repeated decision cards. We considered readability, keyboard and touch controls, reduced motion, lightweight assets and clear separation between scientific evidence and fictional gameplay.

Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space, systems thinking and evidence-based observation. The prototype has undergone software and browser checks; learning outcomes with children have not yet been evaluated.

NASA resources are acknowledged with gratitude. NASA does not endorse this project. Third-party assets and music remain credited to their respective creators. Flight timing, resource balances, hazards and health effects are simplified educational mechanics.
